A fun little Vampire Survivors clone with zom-zoms and cute maids. Pros: -- Fully voice acted (all voices in Japanese) -- Fantastic and varied soundtrack -- Surprisingly good writing (some jokes actually made me laugh out loud) -- Interesting character designs -- Likable characters -- Satisfying gameplay loop -- All characters are fun to use and viable, though 1-2 are definitely OP -- Permanent Upgrade system for armor and weapons Cons: -- The story is good, but the localization is terrible. -- Lots of context errors in menus (ex: the game calls experience points "power") and some achievements aren't worded well at all. -- Very slow character movement, except for one character (note: this can be improved with in-game and permanent upgrades, but it isn't by much) General observations, neither pros nor cons: -- Drones are OP. Nothing else exists that comes close to electric drones with lasers. -- No nudity, just underwear. This apparently makes it a deal-breaker to some people in the forums.

Overall, this is an extremely light recommendation, partly due to the price. Maid of the Dead is a vampire survivors style game with visual novel elements. TL;DR version: If you like Vampire Survivors style games and maids, it's okay if you get it on sale. But you can get far more mechanically complex Survivors-likes at much lower price points. As a visual novel, it's fine. The artwork is nice and each of the girls has interesting quirks. It doesn't go overly deep on the characters and it's a zombie story that doesn't do anything new. If you don't care about the zombie + maid gimmick, you could probably get a better visual novel for the same price. As a Surviviors-like, it's a bit bare bones. I like that the rounds start at only a couple minutes and then eventually reach 30 minutes, unlike Vampire Survivors, where you're locked into the 30 minute run time. I also really like the pixel art. This was great for a couple of minutes of play before bed. But ultimately, there are only two builds: Grenades or Drones. One is viable early game while the other is viable late game. No weapon evolution or fusion. No banishment mechanics. A max of one re-roll. Minimal meta-progression. I DID enjoy playing it, so I ultimately recommend it, but you could absolutely get a better survivors-like experience at a MUCH cheaper price. You can get four copies of the far more content rich Vampire Survivors for the same price. Even if you wanted a sexy survivors like, Beautiful/Sexy Mystic Survivors is more mechanically complex (but less visually polished) at half the price.

Maid of the Dead is a fast-paced arcade action title that blends modern survival-shooter design with anime flair and a tongue-in-cheek premise. Developed by qureate in collaboration with IXILL LLC. and published by qureate, the game drops players into a zombie-overrun Akihabara where combat maids are humanity’s last line of defense. Rather than aiming for grim horror, it embraces stylish chaos and exaggerated presentation, delivering an experience that is loud, energetic, and unapologetically gamey from the moment it begins. The narrative setup is simple but effective, serving primarily as a vehicle for action. A mysterious outbreak has turned the city into a sea of undead, and a group of maids—each armed with a unique combination of firearms and melee weapons—take it upon themselves to push back the infection. The story unfolds in short bursts between missions, offering character banter and light exposition that reinforce the game’s playful tone. While it never becomes the emotional core of the experience, the narrative does enough to establish stakes and personality, ensuring that the action feels contextualized rather than abstract. Gameplay is built around twin-stick shooter fundamentals, with players controlling movement and aiming independently as waves of zombies flood the screen. The controls are immediately intuitive, allowing newcomers to jump in quickly, but the sheer density of enemies demands constant attention and smart positioning. Survival depends on maintaining mobility, managing space, and reacting to threats from all directions, especially as enemy numbers scale rapidly. The moment-to-moment action is relentless, capturing the satisfying tension that defines strong survival shooters. Progression during each run is driven by experience gains and randomized upgrades. Defeating enemies grants levels that unlock new abilities or enhance existing ones, ranging from automated drones and homing shots to area-of-effect attacks and defensive boosts. These upgrades can dramatically change how a run unfolds, encouraging experimentation and adaptability. No two sessions feel exactly the same, as different combinations of skills lead to wildly different power curves and strategies. One of the game’s most distinctive mechanics is the ability to rescue zombified maids using special Unity Bullets. Rather than simply eliminating every enemy, players can choose to convert certain foes into allies, expanding their combat force mid-battle. Recruited maids fight alongside you, adding firepower and absorbing attention from enemy hordes. This system introduces meaningful tactical choices, as rescuing allies often requires risky positioning but can pay off by tipping the balance during intense encounters. Character variety further enhances replayability. Each maid comes with a different loadout and combat style, influencing everything from engagement range to crowd-control potential. Some excel at close-quarters combat with shotguns or melee weapons, while others favor precision rifles or rapid-fire guns. These differences are more than cosmetic, encouraging players to adjust their movement patterns and upgrade priorities depending on who they choose to deploy. Over time, unlocking and mastering different characters becomes a significant source of long-term motivation. Between missions, players can invest in persistent upgrades that carry over across runs. These systems soften the genre’s inherent difficulty curve, allowing gradual improvement even when individual attempts end in failure. Unlocking stronger equipment, additional resources, and enhanced abilities creates a sense of steady growth that balances the randomness of in-run progression. This dual-layer system—short-term builds combined with long-term advancement—helps maintain engagement over extended play sessions. Visually, Maid of the Dead leans into bright anime aesthetics and exaggerated effects. Character designs are colorful and expressive, standing out clearly amid the chaos of the battlefield. Enemy hordes are plentiful and varied enough to keep encounters visually dynamic, even if individual zombie designs are relatively simple. Environments serve as functional backdrops rather than focal points, but they provide enough variation to prevent the experience from feeling visually static. Audio design reinforces the game’s high-energy identity. Weapon effects are punchy and satisfying, while character voice lines add personality and reinforce the anime tone. Music tracks keep the adrenaline high, matching the escalating intensity of each encounter. While the soundtrack is not especially subtle, it complements the game’s arcade sensibilities well. As with many survival shooters, repetition can set in during longer sessions. Enemy patterns and objectives do not change dramatically, and the screen can occasionally become cluttered during peak moments, making it difficult to read every threat. Balance between upgrades and characters can also feel uneven, with certain builds clearly outperforming others depending on luck. However, these issues are largely mitigated by the game’s emphasis on quick runs and constant action rather than prolonged strategic planning. Overall, Maid of the Dead succeeds as a stylish and entertaining entry in the survival shooter genre. It does not aim to redefine the formula, but it executes its ideas with confidence, layering character variety, rescue mechanics, and energetic presentation on top of a proven gameplay foundation. For players who enjoy twin-stick shooters, anime aesthetics, and chaotic battles against overwhelming odds, it offers a satisfying blend of intensity and personality that makes each run feel rewarding, even in defeat. Rating: 7/10

Having played a ton of these types of games (survivors-like "bullet heaven"), I have to say I consider Maid of the Dead one of the weaker ones. I still had fun with it, but there are a few areas where it's lacking. The good: - The art is spectacular. Character portraits and unique cut-scene images are really polished. - All the cut scenes are fully voiced in Japanese. - The six playable characters feel unique enough, with individual guns, melee attacks and special attacks. - There's a level later on where you can kill as many enemies as you want for as long as you want before triggering a boss, making it easier to farm for gold and craft late-game items. The bad: - Environments look bland and generic. - Not many enemy types, and no variation in behavior (outside of bosses). Even the "elite" enemies are just larger versions of regular enemies who take more hits. - The power-ups that make up your build just aren't visually or mechanically interesting. There are a bunch of explosives and a bunch of drones, making for very little visual variation in on-screen action. - While the cut scenes are charming and well-acted, there are so. Many. Of. Them. The game's momentum repeatedly comes to a screeching halt in order to watch our protagonists chit-chat and/or progress the plot. You unlock dozens more cut-scenes you can only watch from the main menu. Heck, you can even unlock new bullet types by watching certain unlocked cut scenes, something I learned far too late for it to be of any use. - Speaking of which, I found the "consumable items" system to be kind of underbaked and not particularly useful. - The game just starts feeling too repetitive after a while. Which, yes, is kind of foundationally true for the entire genre, but there isn't enough variety here (visually or mechanically) to keep it engaging. I had decided I was done with this game long ago, then randomly came back to it recently and decided to sweep up the last few achievements. Don't get me wrong: I did have fun with Maid of the Dead and I found the anime aesthetic very charming (although I found the de-zombifying "treatment" scenes to be incredibly awkward), but there are plenty of better games in the genre (Boneraiser Minions, Halls of Torment, Brotato, Holocure: Save the Fans, the Castlevania DLC for Vampire Survivors, etc). Recommended to those who simply can't get enough of the genre.

It's a Vampire survivor like game with a lot of maid/zombie fanservice that can get really uncomfortable at times. But it does not compare to its inspiration. Limited pool of weapons and upgrades, lack of combining weapons to get better weapons, no enemy types beyond zombie that runs at the player and a vestigial mechanic of being able to convert enemies to fight by your side that is just useless in long run, makes repeated run of the game extremely repetitive and samey. i really gave the game a chance because roguelike waifu VS-like games are generally fun. but this one just wasn't. it's more emphasis on story than anything else. but at that point just invest in a visual novel. i generally don't care for fan service. but normally the gameplay is priority over it in games that have it. but with this game it feels invasive. when you get damaged a certain amount (mainly by zombies dropping from the sky, directly on top of you) you just get this big interruption of the action for a fan service jpeg. normally games with this type of function just show it off to the side without gameplay interruption. the vaccine thing is just more tedious than anything. from a gameplay perspective it's just a waste of time. you could definitely just add the pic to the story and show the maids getting cured via story rather than this mini game. because it's not really fun at all. and finally the gameplay issues. This game does the thing that is the biggest problem with some games of this genre. it's just a stat check game. do a mission. spend currency on upgrades. you don't need to spend it on anything else because it's irrelevant compared to the upgrades for your character's weapons. i haven't died at all playing this game and all i'm doing is spamming upgrades on my character's weapon, and that's it. not buying any items or materials because i get enough per run that there's no need. and as i said before, the accessory items just have near zero enough impact. for a roguelike this is what separates good ones from the mediocre. there are not enough versatile upgrades that make me look forward to going back into a run. because every run is the same. no enemy variety. even with the bosses. they all do the same thing. Sure the presentation of this game is awesome. which is likely what gets people to buy it. But it is severely lacking in substance. and it's a shame that i really committed expecting the game to open up and expand past the 2 hour mark. because i'd definitely have refunded otherwise. This game is closer to maybe a $3-$5 area. because there's just very little gameplay. if the game was marketed as a visual novel with some gameplay elements then expectations would be more realistic.
